What is a stablecoin? A plain-English guide

By the Ibanora teamPublished November 16, 20267 min read

In short

A stablecoin is a crypto token built to hold a steady value, usually one US dollar. Its issuer promises to redeem each token for a fixed amount of money and holds reserves to back that promise. Today people mostly use stablecoins to trade other crypto assets and to send money across borders.

A stablecoin (sometimes written "stable coin") is a crypto token designed to keep a steady price by tracking another asset, almost always a national currency such as the US dollar. For most stablecoins, the issuing company promises to swap each token back for that fixed amount and holds reserves to cover the promise. As of November 16, 2026, stablecoins pegged to the dollar added up to about $283 billion, according to DefiLlama's stablecoin data.

What is a stablecoin?

The Bank of England describes stablecoins as digital assets you can use to make payments, backed by a specified asset or a group of assets. Most are backed by a currency such as the US dollar, and holders can generally exchange them for that value. A technology company can create them; it does not have to be a bank.

US law now has its own definition. The GENIUS Act, signed on July 18, 2025, defines a "payment stablecoin" as a digital asset used, or designed to be used, for payment or settlement. Its issuer must convert or redeem it for a fixed amount of money and says it will keep a stable value against that amount. The definition leaves out national currencies, bank deposits and securities.

Almost all stablecoins track the dollar. In its 2025 annual report, the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) said over 99% of stablecoins were denominated in US dollars.

How stablecoins work

A fiat-backed stablecoin, the most common kind, goes through the same cycle each time:

  1. Someone pays the issuer in full, in the currency the token tracks. The BIS calls this a cash-in-advance constraint: tokens exist only after the money arrives.
  2. The issuer creates the matching number of tokens and holds the money as reserves, for example in a bank account, according to the Bank of England.
  3. The tokens move between wallets on a blockchain. Holders can send them, trade them or keep them.
  4. To cash out, a holder redeems tokens with the issuer for the fixed amount, or sells them to someone else, often through an on-ramp and off-ramp service that converts between tokens and ordinary money.

Because the value rests on the reserves, large issuers publish reports on them. Circle says on its transparency page, as of November 2026, that most USDC reserves sit in the Circle Reserve Fund, an SEC-registered government money market fund that can hold cash, short-dated US Treasuries and overnight Treasury repurchase agreements, and that the rest is cash, mostly at a handful of very large banks. Circle discloses reserve holdings weekly, and a Big Four accounting firm gives monthly assurance that reserves exceed the USDC in circulation (as of November 2026). Tether's transparency page says USDT is backed 100% by Tether's reserves and that its assets exceed its liabilities (as of November 2026).

Types of stablecoins

Stablecoins differ in what sits behind the peg:

  • Fiat-backed stablecoins hold reserves such as cash, bank deposits and short-term government debt, and track one currency at 1 to 1. DefiLlama classifies USDT, USDC, PayPal USD and EURC this way.
  • Commodity-backed tokens track a physical asset. Paxos says each PAX Gold (PAXG) token is backed by one fine troy ounce of London Good Delivery gold (as of November 2026).
  • Crypto-backed stablecoins use other crypto assets as collateral. DefiLlama classifies Sky's USDS and the older DAI this way.
  • Synthetic dollars pair crypto assets with trades that offset their price moves. Ethena describes USDe as a synthetic dollar backed by crypto assets and matching short futures positions, and says it is not a fiat stablecoin like USDC or USDT (as of November 2026).
  • Algorithmic stablecoins try to hold the peg through code and a second token instead of reserves. The SEC says TerraUSD (UST) was meant to keep its dollar peg by being interchangeable with another token, LUNA. UST lost its peg in May 2022, and it and its sister tokens fell to nearly zero.

What are stablecoins used for?

Trading crypto is the main use today. The IMF's December 2025 paper Understanding Stablecoins says crypto trading is the main driver of recent issuance, and the Bank of England names buying and selling other cryptoassets as one of the two main uses.

The other is sending money abroad. The Bank of England says stablecoins are used for cross-border payments that avoid a bank in the middle. The BIS adds that they serve as a payment tool for people in emerging markets with limited access to dollars, and that cross-border volumes tend to rise after periods of high inflation and currency swings. This is the idea behind stablecoin cross-border payments: money is converted to a stablecoin, moved, and converted back.

The IMF sees wider payments and tokenization as possible future uses, if legal and regulatory frameworks allow them. Holding stablecoins takes a stablecoin wallet, which keeps the tokens at an address on a blockchain.

Stablecoins vs cryptocurrency, CBDCs and bank deposits

Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency but not a stablecoin. The Bank of England says Bitcoin is issued by the network's code rather than a company, has no backing assets, and its value can move sharply.

A central bank digital currency (CBDC) is also different. Companies issue stablecoins, while a central bank would issue a CBDC as a digital form of cash. The Bank of England's explainer, last updated in April 2026, says no decision has been made on a UK CBDC, which would be called the digital pound.

Stablecoins are also not bank deposits. The GENIUS Act excludes deposits from its definition of a payment stablecoin. It also says payment stablecoins are not backed by the full faith and credit of the United States and are not covered by federal deposit insurance.

Risks to understand

  • A stablecoin can lose its peg. When Silicon Valley Bank failed in March 2023, Circle had $3.3 billion of USDC reserves there, about 8% of the total. In a March 2023 release, Circle said the dollar de-peg had closed after US authorities said the bank's depositors would be made whole.
  • Designs without full reserves can fail outright, as UST did in May 2022.
  • Each stablecoin carries its issuer's name. The BIS points out that different stablecoins can therefore trade at different rates, even when they track the same currency.
  • Mistakes are hard to fix. The BIS points to a lack of ways to stop or reverse payments made by mistake or through fraud.
  • Countries face risks too. The IMF warns that stablecoins may contribute to currency substitution and capital-flow volatility, especially where inflation is high or confidence in the local currency is low.

How stablecoins are regulated

United States

The GENIUS Act (Public Law 119-27) requires permitted issuers to hold identifiable reserves of at least 1 to 1. Allowed reserves include US coins and currency, bank deposits, Treasury bills, notes or bonds with 93 days or less to maturity, certain overnight repurchase agreements and government money market funds. Issuers must publish the monthly composition of their reserves on their website, and they may not pay holders interest or yield just for holding the stablecoin.

The Act takes effect on the earlier of January 18, 2027 (18 months after enactment) or 120 days after regulators issue final rules. The OCC issued its final rule on October 21, 2026, and OCC Bulletin 2026-50 says it takes effect on January 18, 2027. The OCC's rules on anti-money laundering and sanctions will come in a separate rulemaking, in coordination with the Treasury Department.

European Union

The EU covers stablecoins in its Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA, Regulation (EU) 2023/1114). The European Banking Authority says its rules for issuing and offering stablecoins have applied since June 30, 2024. MiCA has two kinds. An e-money token (EMT) aims to keep a stable value by reference to one official currency. An asset-referenced token (ART) references other values or rights, or a mix of them.

In the EU, only an authorized credit institution or electronic money institution may issue an EMT, according to the EBA. Circle says EURC is issued by Circle Internet Financial Europe SAS, an electronic money institution authorized by France's ACPR, and qualifies as an e-money token under MiCA (as of November 2026). ESMA keeps a public register that lists EMT issuers. Its MiCA page shows that the rules for crypto-asset service providers started on December 30, 2024, with a transition for existing firms that ran until July 1, 2026 at the latest.

United Kingdom

The Bank of England and other UK authorities have proposed rules for stablecoins that are widely used for payments in the UK. Its explainer, last updated in April 2026, says no stablecoin is used that widely yet.

Questions

Do stablecoins pay interest?

Under the US GENIUS Act, a permitted issuer may not pay holders any interest or yield, in cash, tokens or anything else, just for holding or using a payment stablecoin.

What is the largest stablecoin?

Tether (USDT) is the largest by supply. DefiLlama put it at about $175.3 billion on November 16, 2026, around 62% of all dollar stablecoins. USD Coin (USDC) was second at about $69.3 billion.

Is there a stablecoin pegged to the British pound?

Yes, a few exist. The Bank of England says a small number of stablecoins are linked to the pound, though none is yet widely used for payments in the UK.

How can I check whether a stablecoin is authorized in the EU?

The European Banking Authority suggests checking the token's white paper, the issuer's website and ESMA's register. You can also check authorization on the website of the relevant national authority. If an issue or offer does not follow MiCA, its safeguards do not apply.
